heading: Models: types without a role
body:
Data types that several files share live in client/models/ or server/models/. A models folder is not a role folder. A models file holds data, not behavior (ADR 0041, ADR 0043). Choose a language below. TypeScript, JavaScript, Rust, C#, F#, Dart, Kotlin, Go, Java, Ruby, Lua and Python models work in both realms. Swift models live only in client/models/, because Swift is not a Yon language. PHP and Groovy models live only in server/models/, because those languages run only in Yon. The PHP and Groovy tabs show only a route that returns the guide, and the page is not part of them. A Python model is a `@dataclass`, and a Python page service also needs the Python runtime in `client/manifest.json` (see Your first app). A controller returns a model, or takes one with FromBody, and Yon turns it into JSON and back, like Spring.

A JavaScript models file holds one JSDoc `@typedef` comment and `export {}`, such as `client/models/CartTotal.js` for `CartTotal`. Every JavaScript file of the realm uses a JavaScript model by its name, with no import. JavaScript also reads the TypeScript models of its realm: write `/** @import { Guide } from '/models/Guide.ts' */` above the class. Routes, events and `/api.json` read these models like the models of any other language. A `@typedef` in another JavaScript file of client/ or server/ is a model outside its folder. The build refuses it with `TY1310`, and `ty migrate fix --write` moves it to the models folder. The fix keeps one file for identical copies. When a copy matches a model that the realm already has, in JavaScript or TypeScript, the fix removes the copy and imports that model. It reports a copy that differs, and leaves that file for you.

A TypeScript models file holds interfaces, type aliases and import type statements. TypeScript removes a type-only import, so the browser never loads the models file. In the other languages, a models file holds structs, records, data classes, enums and type aliases with fields only. It also holds the imports they need. A PHP array has no item type, so a doc comment gives it: `/** @var list<Guide> */` on a property, or `@param list<Guide> $guides` and `@return list<Guide>` on a controller method. A Ruby model is a Data.define record whose fields have YARD @!attribute types. A Lua model is a table whose fields have `---@field` types.

Every models file holds one model: one interface, type alias, JSDoc `@typedef`, struct, record, class, enum or Ruby record, and the file is named after it, such as `Guide.ts` for `Guide` (ADR 0067). Put a second model, even a small enum, in its own file next to the first. A models file with two models fails with `TY1318`, and `ty migrate fix --write` splits it into one file per model.

Other files import a model in the usual way of their language: `import type { Guide } from '/models/Guide.ts'`, `use crate::models::Guide;`, `using Models;`, `import 'models/Guide.dart';`, `import models.Guide`, `import models.Guide;`, `open Models`, `from models import Guide` or `use Models\Guide;`. JavaScript, Swift, Go, Ruby and Lua use the type name with no import. A C++ model is a `struct` or an `enum class` in a header-only file such as `client/models/Guide.hpp`, and other C++ files may write `#include "../models/Guide.hpp"` so that an editor finds it; C++ models live only in `client/models` (`TY1372`). A Go models file holds one type, because Tachyon compiles it as another file of the program's package main. The framework adds the realm's models files of that language to every program it builds in that language. A JavaScript or TypeScript page service is the exception: its module gets only the models that it names, and the models that those name, so a route does not load the others (ADR 0043). It never routes a models file and never ships one on its own. A Rust model declares its type and fields pub, because the models files become the module crate::models. Each Rust models file is its own module inside it, so a model that uses another model writes `use crate::models::Item;`. When a models file does not compile, the error names that file.

A role annotation in a models folder fails with TY1310. The message names the role folder where the type belongs. A method, a function, a constant or a service marker also fails with TY1310. So does any other statement, or a language in the wrong realm. A model may carry configuration and validation data: Settings, Setting, Checked, Required, NotEmpty, Length, Min, Max and Description (ADR 0092). Every Tac and Yon language reads such a model except Lua, which refuses these markers in a model. A Swift schema model is a struct, and a Rust schema model is `pub`.
